hints: Look carefully at all the labels in Fig. 4.1 and list what is present in the virosome - a phospholipid bilayer plus two glycoproteins.
Recall the two essential internal components that allow a real virus to carry information and protect it, and check if they appear in the diagram.
walkthrough:
What makes a virus able to cause disease**
A complete virus particle must carry genetic material inside to take over a host cell. That nucleic acid is protected by a protein coat called the capsid. Without these, it cannot replicate or cause disease.

What the virosome is missing**
Fig. 4.1 shows only a phospholipid bilayer with haemagglutinin and neuraminidase in the central area. There is no DNA or RNA in the centre and no capsid layer. That is why virosomes do not cause disease but can still look like the outside of influenza virus to the immune system.
Final answer: Virosome has no nucleic acid (DNA/RNA) and no capsid / protein coat. Only some viruses have envelopes, but virosome is essentially envelope only.

hints: Start from the phospholipid bilayer itself - remember which part of a phospholipid loves water and which part avoids water.
Look at which way the phospholipids are facing on the inner side of the virosome in Fig. 4.1 and think about what that tells you about the central area.
walkthrough:
Remembering phospholipid behaviour**
Each phospholipid has a phosphate head that is hydrophilic, meaning it interacts well with water, and two fatty acid tails that are hydrophobic, meaning they avoid water. In water they always arrange so heads face water and tails face away.

Reading the orientation in Fig. 4.1**
In the virosome the bilayer is arranged as a circle. On the inner leaflet the heads point inward toward the central area. Heads would only face that way if water is there to interact with. So the central area must be aqueous.
Final answer: Phosphate heads are hydrophilic and fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. The hydrophilic heads point inward toward the central area, so the central area must contain water / be aqueous.

hints: Think about the job of any vaccine - what must it provide to the immune system without causing disease?
Use the clue that haemagglutinin binds to phagocytes - how would getting taken up by a phagocyte help start a full immune response?
walkthrough:
Vaccines need a safe signal**
A vaccine must look enough like the real pathogen for the immune system to learn from it, but not cause disease. Proteins from the outside of the virus are ideal because they are recognised as non-self.

From binding to memory**
Haemagglutinin in the virosome provides that foreign antigen. Binding to a receptor on phagocytes encourages uptake and antigen presentation, which activates B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes. This gives a primary response and leaves memory cells, so a real influenza infection later gives a fast secondary response.

Final answer: Haemagglutinin acts as a foreign / non-self antigen that triggers a primary immune response giving artificial active immunity, leading to activation of B and T lymphocytes and formation of memory cells.

hints: Link primary structure to protein shape - what level of structure forms the active site and decides which substrate fits?
Think about what would happen to the virus if a mutation changed the active site so neuraminidase could no longer work to release new viruses.
walkthrough:
Why the sequence matters for function**
Primary structure is the amino acid sequence. It determines how the protein folds into its tertiary structure, including the exact shape and chemistry of the active site. Only the correct substrate fits that shape.

Why change is not tolerated here**
Neuraminidase is essential because it lets new viruses leave host cells to infect other cells. If mutation altered amino acids in the active site, the shape would change, substrate would not bind, and the enzyme would fail. Those viruses would not spread, so only viruses keeping the unchanged active-site sequence survive.

Final answer: No change in tertiary structure / shape of active site, so same substrate can still bind and neuraminidase still functions to release virus from host cells. Mutations in the active-site coding region are selected against as the gene is essential.
